title: US formal financial access infrastructure contracted while user-reported account ownership remained high
source_unit: IMF Financial Access Survey annual administrative/provider-reported US series; IMF.STA:FAS(5.0.0)

denominator.unit: provider count; no common population denominator

credit_unions_and_credit_cooperatives.unit: number of credit unions and credit cooperatives

observations.method: IMF SDMX 2.1 CSV query for IMF.STA:FAS(5.0.0), USA, 2020–2024; provider counts transcribed from the returned annual series and changes calculated from first and last observations.
observations.uncertainty: Provider counts are administrative/reporting measures, not unique customer counts or a direct measure of geographic service quality. Definitions, reporting coverage, mergers, charter changes, and revisions can affect the series.
observations.subgroup: US provider type: commercial banks versus credit unions and credit cooperatives; no customer, geography, income, or demographic subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Fewer institutions can coexist with stable or improved digital access, consolidation can change scale, and provider counts do not identify branch closures, prices, account access, or consumer welfare.

denominator.unit: adult-population-normalized provider measure; underlying adult denominator supplied by IMF/country metadata

observations.method: IMF FAS series FA22_COMBANK and FA26N from the same US SDMX response; FA26N selected using adult-normalized PHTADLT_NUM transformation, not the separate square-kilometer series.
observations.uncertainty: The normalized series is not a measure of travel distance, accessibility, branch hours, service quality, or digital substitution. Headquarters are excluded from the branch count, and the series can reflect reporting and institutional changes.
observations.subgroup: US commercial-bank physical network; no place, rurality, income, disability, or customer subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A contracting branch network may accompany more convenient digital service for some customers while imposing travel, identity, cash, or human-contact costs on others; the FAS series cannot determine which route occurred.

denominator.unit: household outstanding balance normalized by US GDP; not a household count

household_outstanding_deposits.unit: percent of GDP; commercial-bank household deposits

household_outstanding_loans.unit: percent of GDP; commercial-bank household loans

observations.method: IMF FAS OUTD_COMBANK_S14 and OUTL_COMBANK_S14 series; observations are reported as ratios to GDP, not dollar balances or household-level rates.
observations.uncertainty: Ratios to GDP can change because balances, GDP, valuation, reporting, or sector classification changed. They do not measure deposit adequacy, loan affordability, delinquency, liquidity, or household welfare.
observations.subgroup: US commercial-bank household-sector balances; no income, age, race, gender, tenure, or account-level subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lower balance-to-GDP ratio is not necessarily less household security; it can reflect denominator growth, portfolio composition, repayment, transfers between institutions, or post-pandemic balance normalization.

denominator.unit: separate provider and adult-survey aggregates; no common person, account, or household denominator

findex_account_ownership_change.unit: percentage points, World Bank Global Findex 2021–2024

observations.method: Descriptive cross-source contrast between IMF provider-side US series and World Bank Global Findex adult-reported account ownership; no pooled estimate or causal join.
observations.uncertainty: The periods, units, definitions, survey/administrative designs, and denominators differ. This contrast cannot attribute account ownership to branch contraction or digital substitution.
observations.subgroup: US provider aggregate versus US adult respondent aggregate; no aligned subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital channels, mergers, credit unions, nonbank providers, and customer behavior may all affect the apparent divergence; the same customer is not followed across the two sources.

related_sources.claim: Global Findex supplies adult-reported account, device, payment, saving, borrowing, and resilience indicators at a different demand-side unit.
SHED supplies US household financial room, hardship, adaptation, and recovery measures not present in provider counts or balance-to-GDP ratios.
OFR supplies financial-system structure and market-plumbing context at a different institutional level.

boundary: The IMF FAS US extract establishes a provider-side contraction in commercial-bank and credit-union counts and commercial-bank branch density from 2020 to 2024, alongside falling household commercial-bank deposit and loan ratios to GDP. The World Bank Findex comparison shows high and rising adult account ownership over a partly overlapping period. The divergence is a measurement result, not proof of digital substitution, reduced welfare, exclusion, or improved access. A same-person/account event design is still needed to connect provider change to household terms, travel, payment success, remedy, trust, switching, or exit.
